lead: Classification is the part of machine learning that assigns a label to a new example. This unit builds the main classifier families: decision trees, Bayesian methods, nearest neighbours, support vector machines, ensembles and local methods. After it, you can choose a classifier for a small dataset, read its assumptions and compute a simple example by hand.
about: The unit starts with decision trees (3.1): entropy and information gain build a tree from labelled rows. Bayes theorem (3.2) supplies the posterior view behind Naive Bayes (3.3), then the ideal Bayes optimal classifier and Gibbs sampling (3.4). Bayesian belief networks (3.5) keep Bayes but drop the strong independence assumption. k-nearest neighbour (3.6) turns stored examples into a classifier. Support vector machines (3.7) replace local voting with a maximum-margin boundary and kernels. Ensembles (3.8) combine many trees or classifiers into bagging, boosting and random forests. The last chapter (3.9) covers locally weighted regression, RBF networks and case-based reasoning, where prediction stays close to the query.

chapters.idea: ID3 grows a decision tree by repeatedly splitting on the attribute with the highest information gain.
chapters.depth: Entropy H(S) = −Σ p_i log₂ p_i measures class mixing in set S; p_i is the fraction of S in class i. Information gain IG(S,A) = H(S) − Σ_v (|S_v|/|S|) H(S_v) is the entropy drop after splitting on attribute A; v runs over A's values and S_v is the subset with value v. ID3 picks the largest IG, makes a branch for each value, and recurses until a node is pure or no attributes remain. Some syllabi call the same idea 'decision tree induction'. Mention C4.5 gain ratio and CART Gini only as names; do not teach pruning here.

figure.aria: A decision tree with root Wind, branch Weak leading to Yes and branch Strong leading to No.

chapters.example: Six days predict Play from Weather and Wind: (Sunny, Weak, Yes), (Sunny, Strong, No), (Rain, Weak, Yes), (Rain, Strong, No), (Sunny, Weak, Yes), (Rain, Weak, Yes). H(S)=− (4/6)log₂(4/6) − (2/6)log₂(2/6)=0.918. Split Weather: Sunny subset has 2 Yes,1 No, H=0.918; Rain subset has 2 Yes,1 No, H=0.918; IG(Weather)=0. Split Wind: Weak subset has 4 Yes,0 No, H=0; Strong subset has 0 Yes,2 No, H=0; IG(Wind)=0.918. ID3 picks Wind; the tree has root Wind, branch Weak→Yes, branch Strong→No.
chapters.trap: A high-branch attribute can get high gain just by many values; information gain is biased. Do not split on an ID or row number.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: concept learning and basic probability.
chapters.leave: Pruning, missing values, continuous splits and regression trees go to later reading; ensembles use trees in 3.8.

chapters.idea: Bayes theorem combines prior belief with observed likelihood to give a posterior; MAP uses the posterior, MLE uses only the likelihood.
chapters.depth: Bayes theorem: P(h|D)=P(D|h)P(h)/P(D). h is a hypothesis, D is observed data, P(h) is prior, P(D|h) is likelihood, P(h|D) is posterior, and P(D) normalizes. MAP picks h_MAP=argmax_h P(D|h)P(h). MLE picks h_MLE=argmax_h P(D|h); it is MAP with a uniform prior. For a coin with unknown bias p, the likelihood of h heads in n tosses is C(n,h)p^h(1−p)^(n−h); C(n,h) is the binomial coefficient. Some syllabi call MLE 'maximum likelihood estimation' and MAP 'maximum a posteriori'.

figure.aria: A plot with two hypotheses on x; h2 has higher likelihood, but h1 has higher posterior after the prior.

chapters.example: Ten tosses give 7 heads. h1: p=0.5; h2: p=0.8. P(D|h1)=C(10,7)(0.5)^10=120/1024=0.1172. P(D|h2)=120(0.8)^7(0.2)^3=0.2013. MLE is h2. If priors are P(h1)=0.9, P(h2)=0.1, posterior scores are 0.9×0.1172=0.1055 and 0.1×0.2013=0.0201; MAP is h1. The prior flips the choice.
chapters.trap: Do not call P(D|h) the posterior; MAP includes the prior. P(D) can be dropped only when comparing hypotheses for the same data.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 probability: conditional probability and distributions.
chapters.leave: EM for hidden variables is Unit 4; Bayesian networks are 3.5.

chapters.idea: Naive Bayes classifies by combining the class prior with feature likelihoods, assuming features are independent given the class.
chapters.depth: Naive Bayes assumes features x_1,...,x_n are conditionally independent given class C. It scores each class by P(C)Π_i P(x_i|C); the denominator P(x) is the same for all classes and is dropped. Categorical features use counts; Gaussian Naive Bayes uses a normal density per class and feature. Add Laplace smoothing P(x_i=a|C)=(count(a,C)+α)/(count(C)+α·V); α is the smoothing constant and V is the number of values of that feature. Some syllabi call it 'idiot Bayes'.

figure.aria: A naive Bayes graph with class as parent of Weather and Wind.

chapters.example: Use the six-day data from 3.1 and classify (Weather=Sunny, Wind=Strong) with α=1. Priors: P(Yes)=4/6=0.667, P(No)=2/6=0.333. With smoothing, for Yes: P(Sunny|Yes)=(2+1)/(4+2)=0.5, P(Strong|Yes)=(0+1)/(4+2)=0.167, score=0.667×0.5×0.167=0.0556. For No: P(Sunny|No)=(1+1)/(2+2)=0.5, P(Strong|No)=(2+1)/(2+2)=0.75, score=0.333×0.5×0.75=0.125. Predict No.
chapters.trap: A zero count makes the whole product zero; smooth. Independence is an assumption, not a fact. Unnormalized scores are not probabilities.
chapters.leave: Correlated features and network structure are 3.5; text pipelines are not here.

chapters.idea: The Bayes optimal classifier averages every hypothesis's vote by its posterior weight; Gibbs samples one hypothesis and uses it.
chapters.depth: The Bayes optimal classifier predicts the label c with largest P(c|x,D)=Σ_h P(c|x,h)P(h|D). h is a hypothesis, D is training data, P(h|D) is its posterior, and P(c|x,h) is the vote of h for label c. It averages over the whole hypothesis space, so it is an ideal, not a usual trained model. Gibbs algorithm draws one hypothesis h at random from P(h|D) and predicts with that h. Only a few universities teach Gibbs in detail; know the sampling rule and that it is randomized. Some syllabi call the first 'Bayes optimal classifier'.

figure.aria: Three hypotheses point to their predictions; Bayes optimal adds posterior mass 0.7 on Yes and 0.3 on No.

chapters.example: Three hypotheses have posteriors P(h1|D)=0.5, P(h2|D)=0.3, P(h3|D)=0.2. On test x, h1 and h3 predict Yes; h2 predicts No. Bayes optimal P(Yes)=0.5+0.2=0.7 and P(No)=0.3, so it predicts Yes. Gibbs samples h1 with probability 0.5, h2 with 0.3, h3 with 0.2; it predicts Yes with probability 0.7 and No with 0.3.
chapters.trap: Bayes optimal is not the single MAP hypothesis. Gibbs is not majority vote; it samples one hypothesis.
chapters.leave: Model averaging in ensembles is 3.8; inference in networks is 3.5.

chapters.idea: A Bayesian belief network stores a joint probability as a product of local conditional probabilities on a directed acyclic graph.
chapters.depth: A Bayesian belief network is a directed acyclic graph. Each node is a random variable X_i; each edge points from a parent to a child. The joint probability is P(X_1,...,X_n)=Π_i P(X_i | parents(X_i)). Each node stores a conditional probability table (CPT) for its parents. The graph encodes conditional independencies. Inference means computing a query probability from the joint, by enumeration or variable elimination. Some syllabi call this a 'Bayes net' or 'belief network'.

figure.aria: A Bayesian belief network Fear to Study to Pass, with conditional probability tables on the edges.

chapters.trap: A CPT is P(child|parents), not P(parents|child). Do not create cycles. P(Pass) needs a sum over Study, not just one CPT row.
chapters.leave: Learning CPTs with hidden variables uses EM in Unit 4; approximate inference is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: kNN stores training examples and labels a query by the majority vote of its k nearest stored neighbours.
chapters.depth: kNN stores the training set. For a query x, compute a distance d(x,x_i), often Euclidean d=√Σ_j (x_j−x_ij)²; x_j is the query's j-th feature and x_ij is the stored example's j-th feature. Take the k smallest distances and predict the majority class; for regression take the mean. Distance-weighted kNN gives weight 1/d or 1/(d+ε). k is a positive integer; use an odd k for two classes to avoid ties. Voronoi diagrams show the regions for 1NN. kNN is lazy: no model is built until prediction. Some syllabi call it 'instance-based learning' or 'memory-based learning'.

figure.aria: A query point Q with its three nearest neighbours B, A and D; B and A are positive and D is negative.

chapters.example: Training points: A(1,1)+, B(2,1)+, C(4,4)−, D(4,3)−, E(5,4)−. Query Q(2,2), k=3. Distances: B=1.00, A=1.41, D=2.24, C=2.83, E=3.61. Three nearest are B+, A+, D−. Majority vote gives +. Distance weights: B=1.00, A=0.707, D=0.447; positive total 1.707, negative total 0.447; weighted vote gives +.
chapters.trap: Scale features first; a large-range feature dominates distance. k=1 overfits, large k underfits. Do not tune k on test data.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 distance and data representation; Unit 2 cross-validation for choosing k.
chapters.leave: Weighted local regression is 3.9; high-dimensional distance problems link to PCA in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A support vector machine finds the separating boundary with the largest margin and can use kernels for non-linear boundaries.
chapters.depth: Linear SVM: find w and b for hyperplane w·x+b=0. Labels y_i∈{−1,+1}. The maximum-margin problem is minimize ½||w||² subject to y_i(w·x_i+b)≥1 for all i. ||w|| is the length of w; the margin width is 2/||w||. Points with equality are support vectors. Soft margin adds slack ξ_i≥0 and a cost C: minimize ½||w||²+CΣξ_i subject to y_i(w·x_i+b)≥1−ξ_i. The dual uses only dot products; the kernel trick replaces x_i·x_j by K(x_i,x_j)=φ(x_i)·φ(x_j). Common kernels: polynomial (x·z+1)^d and RBF exp(−γ||x−z||²); d is degree and γ is width. Some syllabi list the quadratic programming solution; know the form, not a full QP solve.

figure.aria: One-dimensional SVM: negative support vector at 0, boundary at 1, positive support vector at 2, each gap 1.

chapters.example: One feature: negative point x=0, positive point x=2. Use y=−1 at 0 and y=+1 at 2. Support-vector equations: w·0+b=−1 and w·2+b=+1. Subtract: 2w=2, so w=1; b=−1. Boundary w x+b=0 gives x=1. Margin=2/||w||=2. Both points are support vectors.
chapters.trap: Margin is 2/||w||, not ||w||. Scaling w and b together changes the equation but not the boundary; the constraints fix the scale. Kernel computes similarity; you do not need φ explicitly.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 linear classifiers and logistic regression; Unit 1 vectors and dot products.
chapters.leave: Full QP derivation, multiclass SVM and SVR are beyond this chapter; neural networks are Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Ensembles combine many models: bagging and random forests reduce variance, while boosting reduces bias by reweighting mistakes.
chapters.depth: Bagging draws B bootstrap samples (sampling with replacement), trains one base model on each, and votes or averages. It mainly reduces variance. Random forests are bagged trees that also choose a random subset of features at each split; this decorrelates trees. Boosting trains models in sequence; AdaBoost starts with weights w_i=1/N, finds a weak classifier h_t, computes error ε_t=Σ_i w_i·1[h_t(x_i)≠y_i], and sets α_t=½ln((1−ε_t)/ε_t). α_t is the classifier's vote weight, N is the number of examples, and 1[...] is 1 if true else 0. It then multiplies weights of wrong examples by exp(α_t) and renormalizes. Final prediction is sign(Σ_t α_t h_t(x)). More rounds reduce bias but can overfit noise. Some syllabi call bagging 'bootstrap aggregating'.

figure.aria: AdaBoost weights before and after one round; point x=3, which was misclassified, rises to 0.5.

chapters.example: Four points: x=1+, x=2+, x=3−, x=4−. Initial weights are 0.25 each. Weak classifier h predicts + for x≤3 and − for x>3. It is wrong only at x=3, so ε=0.25. α=0.5 ln((1−0.25)/0.25)=0.5 ln 3=0.549. Wrong point weight becomes 0.25e^0.549=0.433; each correct point becomes 0.25e^−0.549=0.144. Sum=0.866. Normalized: x=3 weight 0.5; x=1,2,4 weights 0.167 each.
chapters.trap: Bagging does not use misclassification weights; boosting does. Random forest's feature subset is at each split, not just row sampling. Do not evaluate on bootstrap samples only.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 decision trees; Unit 2 bias-variance and cross-validation.
chapters.leave: Stacking and Bayesian model averaging are named in some syllabi but not detailed here; gradient boosting is outside.

chapters.idea: Local methods keep prediction close to the query by weighting nearby points, radial basis functions, or similar past cases.
chapters.depth: Locally weighted regression (LWR) fits a model separately for each query x. Gaussian weight for training point x_i: w_i=exp(−(x_i−x)²/(2τ²)); τ is the bandwidth. Solve weighted least squares at x, often a local linear fit, and predict there. RBF network: hidden unit j has activation φ_j(x)=exp(−||x−μ_j||²/(2σ_j²)); μ_j is its centre and σ_j its width. Output is Σ_j w_j φ_j(x), with output weights w_j. Case-based reasoning (CBR) keeps past cases, retrieves similar ones by a similarity measure, reuses or adapts their solution, revises if needed, and retains the new case. Only a few universities teach RBF networks in this unit; know the formula and one use.

figure.aria: A query at x=1 with Gaussian weights 0.61, 1.00 and 0.61 on points at x=0,1,2; the local prediction is 2.28.

chapters.example: Points (0,1),(1,2),(2,4). Query x=1, τ=1. Gaussian weights: w_0=exp(−1/2)=0.607, w_1=1, w_2=exp(−1/2)=0.607. A weighted linear fit gives prediction y≈2.28 at x=1. The nearest point x=1 has weight 1; the two outer points each have weight 0.607.
chapters.trap: LWR is lazy: weights and fit are recomputed for every query. RBF network is not the SVM RBF kernel. CBR needs a similarity measure; poor features break retrieval.
chapters.prereq: 3.6 kNN; Unit 2 weighted least squares and regression.
chapters.leave: Full RBF training and backpropagation are Unit 5; SVM kernels are 3.7.
